     1	# Lark - a parsing toolkit for Python
     2	
     3	Lark is a parsing toolkit for Python, built with a focus on ergonomics, performance and modularity.
     4	
     5	Lark can parse all context-free languages. To put it simply, it means that it is capable of parsing almost any programming language out there, and to some degree most natural languages too.
     6	
     7	**Who is it for?**
     8	
     9	   - **Beginners**: Lark is very friendly for experimentation. It can parse any grammar you throw at it, no matter how complicated or ambiguous, and do so efficiently. It also constructs an annotated parse-tree for you, using only the grammar and an input, and it gives you convienient and flexible tools to process that parse-tree.
    10	
    11	   - **Experts**: Lark implements both Earley(SPPF) and LALR(1), and several different lexers, so you can trade-off power and speed, according to your requirements. It also provides a variety of sophisticated features and utilities.
    12	
    13	**What can it do?**
    14	
    15	 - Parse all context-free grammars, and handle any ambiguity gracefully
    16	 - Build an annotated parse-tree automagically, no construction code required.
    17	 - Provide first-rate performance in terms of both Big-O complexity and measured run-time (considering that this is Python ;)
    18	 - Run on every Python interpreter (it's pure-python)
    19	 - Generate a stand-alone parser (for LALR(1) grammars)
    20	
    21	And many more features. Read ahead and find out!
    22	
    23	Most importantly, Lark will save you time and prevent you from getting parsing headaches.

   128	---
   129	
   130	Although command line shims are provided, the library is intended to be used
   131	programmatically. Users of the library should instantiate the
   132	``scim2_filter_parser.queries.SQLQuery`` class with an attribute map and optionally
   133	any joins necessary to make all required fields accessible in the query.
   134	
   135	For example, if user information is stored in the ``users`` table and email
   136	information is stored in a different table ``emails``, then the attribute map
   137	and the joins might be defined as so::
   138	
   139	    attr_map = {

   141	        ('name', 'familyName', None): 'users.family_name',
   142	        ('meta', 'lastModified', None): 'users.update_ts',
   143	        ('emails', None, None): 'emails.address',
   144	        ('emails', 'value', None): 'emails.address',
   145	    }
   146	
   147	    joins = (
   148	        'LEFT JOIN emails ON emails.user_id = users.id',
   149	    )
   150	
   151	    q = SQLQuery(filter, 'users', attr_map, joins)
   152	
   153	    q.sql # Will be equal to 'SELECT * FROM users ...
   154	    q.params # Will be equal to the paramters specific to the filter query.
   155	
   156	
   157	The attribute_map (``attr_map``) is a mapping of SCIM attribute, subattribute,
   158	and schema uri to a table field. You will need to customize this to your
   159	particular database schema.

   161	The ``SQLQuery.sql`` method returns SQL that can be used as the first
   162	argument in a call to ``cursor.execute()`` with your favorite DB engine.
   163	If you are using a database that requires a replacement character other than '%s',
   164	then you can subclass the ``SQLQuery`` class and override the ``placeholder`` class
   165	level variable. See the query module and unit tests for an example of this subclassing
   166	with SQLite.
   167	
   168	The ``SQLQuery.params`` method returns a list of items that can be used as the
   169	second argument in a call to ``cursor.execute()``.

   174	In your program, just call the method ``get_query(scim_query: str, attr_map: Mapping)``

"""
Demonstration of the NamedTuple improvement.
Shows how users can now access attribute path components by name.
"""

from src.scim2_filter_parser.attr_paths import AttrPath

def demo_improvement():
    """Demonstrate the improvement in code readability."""
    
    attr_map = {
        ('userName', None, None): 'users.username',
        ('name', 'familyName', None): 'users.family_name',
        ('emails', 'type', None): 'emails.type',
        ('emails', 'value', None): 'emails.address',
        ('urn:example:schema:User', 'customAttr', None): 'custom_attributes.value',
    }
    
    print("=== NamedTuple Improvement Demo ===\n")
    
    # Complex filter demonstrating all three components
    filter_query = 'urn:example:schema:User:customAttr eq "special_value"'
    print(f"Filter: {filter_query}")
    
    attr_path_obj = AttrPath(filter_query, attr_map)
    paths = list(attr_path_obj)
    path = paths[0]
    
    print(f"Path object: {path}")
    print(f"Type: {type(path)}")
    print()
    
    # OLD WAY (index-based access - less readable)
    print("--- Old Way (Index-based access) ---")
    print(f"Attribute name: {path[0]}")
    print(f"Sub-attribute: {path[1]}")
    print(f"URI/schema: {path[2]}")
    print()
    
    # NEW WAY (name-based access - much more readable!)
    print("--- New Way (Named access) ---")
    print(f"Attribute name: {path.attr_name}")
    print(f"Sub-attribute: {path.sub_attr}")
    print(f"URI/schema: {path.uri}")
    print()
    
    # Demonstrate the benefit in real-world usage
    print("--- Real-world usage benefit ---")
    print("# Instead of writing confusing code like:")
    print(f"# if path[2] is not None:  # What is [2] again?")
    print("#     handle_uri_case(path[2])")
    print()
    print("# You can now write self-documenting code:")
    print(f"# if path.uri is not None:")
    print(f"#     handle_uri_case(path.uri)")
    print()
    
    # Multiple paths example
    print("=== Multiple Paths Example ===")
    complex_filter = 'emails[type eq "work" and value co "@company.com"]'
    print(f"Filter: {complex_filter}")
    
    attr_path_obj = AttrPath(complex_filter, attr_map)
    paths = list(attr_path_obj)
    
    for i, path in enumerate(paths):
        print(f"Path {i+1}: {path}")
        print(f"  - Named access: attr='{path.attr_name}', sub='{path.sub_attr}', uri='{path.uri}'")
    
    print()
    print("=== Backward Compatibility ===")
    print("Existing code that uses index access still works!")
    print(f"First path: {paths[0]}")
    print(f"Still equals tuple: {paths[0] == ('emails', 'type', None)}")
    
    # Show it's still hashable
    lookup_dict = {path: f"processed_{i}" for i, path in enumerate(paths)}
    print(f"Still hashable and usable as dict keys: {len(lookup_dict)} entries created")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo_improvement()
